extracted.intended_audience: central and local government officials, regulatory policymakers, and regulatory reviewers in Korea
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive standards for drafting, reviewing, consulting on, implementing and evaluating regulations in the Republic of Korea, including RIA, stakeholder engagement, review bodies, delivery and compliance mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to conduct RIA for primary legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: For primary legislation that contains regulation, a central administrative agency is required to conduct RIA, make an advance notice of the proposed legislation, engage stakeholders in the RIA process, conduct an internal regulatory review, and submit the RIA statement to the RRC for a final review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the RRC review the bill is submitted to the Ministry of Legislation for legislative review, then to the Vice-Ministers Meeting, State Council Meeting and finally to the National Assembly. This full sequence (RIA → advance notice → internal review → RRC review → legislative review → cabinet/assembly steps) is mandatory for primary laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures for secondary legislation (exemption from National Assembly enactment)
rubrics_metrics.description: For secondary legislation that contains regulation, all of the aforementioned procedures are required, except for the enactment procedure of the National Assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary legislation is finalised within the executive branch; it still requires RIA, advance notice, internal review and RRC/other reviews as applicable but does not proceed to the National Assembly.

rubrics_metrics.name: RIA statement (RIAS) content requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Drafted RIAS must contain the outline of regulation, comparison of alternatives to the proposed regulation, cost-benefit analysis, and stakeholder opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The central administrative agency is obligated to publish the RIAS on the official gazette and its webpage during the advance notice period and to collect and feed stakeholder opinions into regulatory bills, then conduct internal review through the agency’s regulatory reform committee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance notice period and publication obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Making an advance notice for 40 days and publishing the RIAS on the official gazette and agency webpage during that advance notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 40-day advance notice gives stakeholders and the general public time to review the RIAS and submit opinions; agencies must collect opinions and provide feedback accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder engagement requirement under the Framework Act
rubrics_metrics.description: When the head of a central administrative agency intends to establish a new regulation or reinforce existing regulations, he or she shall sufficiently consult the opinions of stakeholders such as administrative agencies, civic groups, research institutes and experts by means of public hearing and advance notice of proposed legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct stakeholders are consulted even prior to drafting a bill; engagement includes public hearings and use of other offline and online channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Reform Sinmungo petition handling timelines and obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a petition is filed to the Sinmungo, the public official in charge must respond to the petitioner within 14 days whether to accept the petition or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If rejected petitions are deemed reasonable by the RRO, the responsible agency must justify refusal within three months; urgent petitions require feedback within one week, and if an urgent petition is rejected but deemed reasonable by the RRO the agency must justify within one month. If refusal rationale is insufficient, the RRC can issue recommendations for regulatory improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online platforms and publication of regulatory information
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of online channels (Regulatory Information Portal, Regulatory Reform Sinmungo, e-Legislation Centre) to publish RIA statements, regulatory information and to provide channels for petitions and public comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Regulatory Information Portal publishes all RIA statements and regulatory review information and includes user-customised search by theme, life stage, daily issues etc.; the e-Legislation Centre allows the public to propose a bill and submit opinions, which must be delivered to the relevant agency with required feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal regulatory reform committee: composition and role
rubrics_metrics.description: An internal regulatory reform committee in each central administrative agency amends and substantiates the RIA statement (RIAS) with additional or necessary evidence based on quantified data and stakeholders’ opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The committee is composed of 10 to 20 members representing government and non-government sectors, with non-government experts forming a simple majority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of regulations and review modalities (preliminary/ general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary (online) review classifies bills into significant and less significant regulation; general (in-person) review is conducted on significant regulatory bills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary online screening is used for most proposals; the RRC conducts in-person deliberations bi-weekly on around eight significant proposals and online reviews on many others.

rubrics_metrics.name: RRC mandate, composition and decision authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The RRC is the final decision-making and central oversight body mandated to coordinate and deliberate on (i) direction-setting for regulatory reform policy and R&D of the regulatory system; (ii) review of regulations to be established or reinforced; (iii) review of existing regulations and comprehensive reform plans; (iv) registration and announcement of regulations; (v) stakeholder engagement in regulatory improvement; (vi) inspection and evaluation of regulatory reform efforts; and (vii) other issues deemed necessary by the chairperson.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The RRC comprises Economic and Administrative & Social Sub-Committees, includes government and non-government members (part-time), meets twice a month, and can decide to ‘approve’, ‘recommend revision’, or ‘withdraw’ regulatory proposals. Without RRC clearance a regulatory proposal cannot be enacted.

rubrics_metrics.name: RRO responsibilities in review and mediation
rubrics_metrics.description: The RRO determines whether the proposed bill is subject to regulatory review, mediates and resolves inter-agency conflicts over regulatory direction/content/degree, and determines the necessity of additional impact assessments on SMEs, competition and technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RRO acts as secretariat for the RRC and can request SMBA, FTC and KATS to perform additional reviews if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional impact assessments on SMEs, competition and technology
rubrics_metrics.description: If necessary, an additional RIA on SMEs, competition and technology is requested to SMBA, FTC, and KATS, respectively; these agencies have Regulatory Reform Task Forces to provide expert opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RRO can request such specialist assessments during the regulatory review process to substantiate and improve the quality of RIA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification and clearance of cost-benefit analysis (KDI and KIPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory research centres at KDI and KIPA verify the validity of RIA with particular focus on cost-benefit analysis; KDI assesses RIAS from economic agencies while KIPA assesses RIAS from social and administrative agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KDI/KIPA perform in-depth review of cost-benefit analysis for regulations under the scope of CICO; they can issue a clearance required to continue the review process, or return the analysis for partial or complete revision if errors or ambiguity are found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical Committee on Regulatory Cost and CICO applicability testing
rubrics_metrics.description: A Technical Committee on Regulatory Cost (Regulatory Reform Committee) tests the robustness of cost-benefit analysis in RIA/CICO and conducts final reviews on cost-benefit analysis when regulation falls under the scope of CICO (Cost-in, Cost-out).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination whether a drafted bill is subject to CICO is part of the procedural information; robust CBA is required and subject to testing by the technical committee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory delivery: delegated enforcement channels
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory enforcement may be carried out directly by central administrative agencies, via regional offices, delegated to local regional or sub-regional governments, or entrusted to non-government bodies by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delivery procedure must be specified and may follow different chains (central agency → regional office → regulated entities; or central agency → local regional government → sub-regional government → regulated entities; or delegation to non-government bodies such as Korea Occupational Safety and Health Agency).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measures to raise regulatory compliance (survey dimensions and policy responses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory compliance measurement includes survey items: awareness, comprehension, clarity, necessity, adequacy (fitness-for-purpose), conformity and enforcement; each item has associated measures to raise compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures include informative promotion programmes (awareness); policy promotion, seminars and simplification of legal terms (comprehension); use of plain language, clear stipulation of legal basis, and provision of clear examples (clarity); review of reasonability, public support and cost-benefit analysis for abolition (necessity); consideration of alternatives and priority-driven approach emphasizing non-regulatory options (adequacy); differentiation of regulatory intensity according to conformity levels; adoption of non-command-and-control measures (self-regulation, voluntary agreements, economic inducement); and enhancement of effectiveness of penalties (adequacy of penalty imposition).

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority-driven regulatory design and non-command-and-control alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a priority-driven approach to regulatory design which gives priority to non-regulatory alternatives first, then to regulatory alternatives; consider non-‘command and control’ enforcement measures such as self-regulation, voluntary agreements and economic inducement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When regulation is necessary, consider other alternatives and differentiate regulatory intensity based on compliance levels; this is part of ensuring fitness for purpose and improving conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal channels for regulatory enforcement decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple appeal avenues: (i) Regulatory Reform Sinmungo e-petition system where petitioners can request amendment or explanation and RRC can recommend revisions; (ii) civil petition for grievance to the Anti-Corruption and Civil Rights Commission which can review and recommend rescission or amendment; (iii) Administrative Appeals Commission for narrower issues requiring substantive evidence, which can mandate revocation, affirm nullity, or demand action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any individual or business may use these channels; the Administrative Appeals Commission handles more judicial-like evidentiary matters and issues binding decisions to administrative agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: RIA capacity-building, training and mandatory courses
rubrics_metrics.description: Various training and consulting programmes provided by RRO, NHI, Local Government Officials Development Institute, KDI and KIPA to improve public officials’ capacity for RIA; courses include online and offline syllabi covering necessity, significance, institutional framework, behavioural change, regulatory registry, improvement of existing regulations, review process, RIA and CICO, local government reform and international lessons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training is designed to make public officials draft RIA statements on actual cases on the spot; from 2017 mandatory RIA training was planned for around 400 newly recruited deputy directors and 1,700 newly promoted to deputy director level, plus specified high-level officials and regulatory officers.
